newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Peters defends NZ RSS scheme against early critics.
newsitem.headline: Peters defends NZ RSS scheme against early critics.

text.p: New Zealand Treasurer Winston Peters on Monday rejected as too low estimates of those who would be able to save up to the NZ$120,000 needed under his proposed compulsory retirement savings scheme (RSS).
"I think over nine out of ten men, long term, will be able to save the required amount," Peters told reporters.

Officials have estimated 60 percent of men and only 15 per cent of women will save the required level from their taxable earnings, but Peters said their estimates did not take into account the changes in behaviour his scheme would bring about.
Peters on Monday released details of the proposed scheme in a White Paper. RSS will be put to a referendum in September and the government has said it will be bound by the outcome.
One of the most frequent media criticisms of the scheme has been that it moves the management of funds into a private sector which the government is not prepared to guarantee.

The Treasurer's comments earlier in the day had appeared to signal that he expected the industry to arrange reinsurance, but Peters said ongoing negotiations were rather related to establishing an industry-wide mutual protection system against fraud and failure.
"We are talking not about reinsurance. Industry coverage of its membership would be at much lesser cost. That is probably the path we will take," he told reporters.
He said the government actuary would define various principles fund managers would have to work under.
While Peters argued the scheme would be good for the economy, he acknowledged it would probably slow debt repayment initially but saw it allowing faster debt repayment in the long-term.
"I think it will be very very sound in terms of its effect on the economy. This is a scheme to take people using their own money, to self-reliance. Frankly I don't think we have a choice."
Asked what effect a "yes" vote in the refernedum would have on growth, he said with a smile he would expect it to increase.

He said he expected support for the proposal from government MPs who had in the past been critical of a compulsory scheme, including State Services Minister Jenny Shipley, now that he had addressed their concerns about equity for women.
